criteria: Ranked for a first consumer privacy-request product by public-listing exposure, how much of the workflow was actually inspected, whether the geography matches the catalog, and how much human work remains. Ease alone is not the rank. No record is an unattended automation candidate: every promising web form still has a human step or an unknown verification step.

candidates.name: Spokeo
candidates.why: Direct GET returned the opt-out form. It asks for the public profile URL and an email, then a confirmation link. The page says 24-48 hours and that listings can reappear and must be removed one URL at a time. Spokeo (data) uses the same URL. CAPTCHA was not present on the parsed form; a later step could still add one.

candidates.name: CheckPeople
candidates.why: Direct GET parsed a suppression-tool email field and no login field. Information.com exposes the same single email-field shape. CAPTCHA was not in the parsed HTML and is not proven absent. The rest of the suppression flow was not walked.

candidates.name: CocoFinder
candidates.why: Direct GET of the remove-my-info page parsed a name-or-phone search field. cocofinder.net has the same parsed field on its own URL, so it is a second submission target with the same shape, not proof that one request covers both domains.

candidates.name: GladIKnow
candidates.why: Parsed name, city, and state fields. The same form structure appears on GovernmentRegistry.org, which is also a two-brand shared URL. Email verification is indicated. Build one adapter for this form family and keep each URL as its own submission.

candidates.name: USPhoneBook
candidates.why: The opt-out page states a CAPTCHA, an emailed link, name and phone fields, and about three days to process. unitedstatesphonebook-usphonebook points at a second USPhoneBook URL with the same parsed shape. High phone-listing exposure, with two human gates.

candidates.name: NumLookup
candidates.why: Direct GET parsed phone, full name, and state on a sale opt-out form, with a phone method also published. No CAPTCHA widget was parsed. Confirmation behavior after submit is unknown because nothing was submitted.

candidates.name: SearchUSAPeople
candidates.why: Direct GET parsed a data-removal form with first name, last name, city, and state. The catalog name links it to InfoTracer; that ownership was not re-proven on this page. InfoTracer's own opt-out URL was only a privacy-policy contact path.

candidates.name: PublicRecords.info
candidates.why: Parsed fields include a request-type select, an email, a declaration checkbox, and a full-name search. Useful where one site offers more than one request type. Later confirmation steps were not opened.

candidates.name: PeopleConnect suppression portal
candidates.why: Highest brand leverage in the catalog: many rows share suppression.peopleconnect.us. The page says the tool covers public name-search data on PeopleConnect people-search sites and explicitly excludes Classmates.com and user data. The research GET was an empty shell. A rendered reader showed Start Here, Identity, and Suppression Settings, but those forms were not opened. Do not ship this adapter until the form fields are inspected.

candidates.name: Arrests.org state request portals
candidates.why: Representative of the WPForms request-portal family. About 20 state arrest sites share one field structure and about 9 share another. Form ids differ and each URL is its own submission. A CAPTCHA marker was present. This removes a commercial repost of an arrest record, not the government record.

candidates.name: Sterling
candidates.why: Background-check privacy form with parsed first name, last name, email, and address. A CAPTCHA marker was present. Relevant to employment-screening exposure rather than a casual people-search listing.

candidates.name: FastPeopleSearch
candidates.why: The official instructions are unusually specific: CAPTCHA, emailed link that expires in 24 hours, record form, confirmation page, and about three days. The research GET was blocked by Cloudflare. A rendered reader supplied the instructions. No selectors were captured. High exposure, poor direct access.

candidates.name: Whitepages
candidates.why: Only step 1 of 5 was visible: paste the profile URL. 411.com shares the URL. The research GET was a Cloudflare challenge. Catalog claims of a phone code were not on the inspected step and stay unverified.

candidates.name: Acxiom
candidates.why: US opt-out, access, and deletion are described, with email confirmation, phone, and mail, and processing within two weeks after the confirmation. No request form fields were parsed, so this is a guided manual flow, not a filled form. Strong marketing-data coverage, weaker UI inspection.

candidates.name: OptOutPrescreen
candidates.why: One official firm-offer opt-out for Equifax, Experian, Innovis, and TransUnion. Five years can be requested electronically; permanent opt-out is by mail. It does not delete other bureau data. The research GET was HTTP 403. A rendered reader saw the explanation, not the form fields. A 403 here is not proof that a residential proxy is required.

candidates.name: LexisNexis Risk Solutions
candidates.why: The consumer portal separates direct marketing, FCRA prescreen lists, and public-safety suppression. Safety suppression requires documents. A LexisNexis prescreen opt-out does not cover Equifax, TransUnion, or Experian. Online, mail, and phone are offered. Online fields were not parsed.

candidates.name: Equifax
candidates.why: Step 1 asks for name and address. Date of birth, SSN or ITIN, email, and mobile are optional. Step 2, labeled Verify, was not opened. The page says any US state may use this sale or sharing opt-out and that the FCRA credit report is unaffected. The research GET was an empty shell; a rendered reader showed the form. Do not automate SSN collection.

candidates.name: LiveRamp
candidates.why: Opt-out is described for any US resident. Access, correction, and deletion are limited to states the page lists and, for access and deletion, require identity evidence. The page says deletion and opt-out have different effects and publishes a phone tree. Cookie and device opt-outs are a separate browser-specific path. Not a first unattended adapter.

candidates.name: California DROP
candidates.why: Official one-request path to registered California data brokers, limited to California residents and the state identity gateway. Brokers must check DROP at least every 45 days starting August 1, 2026, and status can take up to 90 days. It does not map one-to-one onto this catalog. The research GET hit Cloudflare. High leverage, not a per-broker form filler.

candidates.name: Social Catfish
candidates.why: Parsed opt-out fields include email, address, a password login, and a profile-style input, plus a CAPTCHA marker. Real people-search exposure, but login and CAPTCHA make it a later adapter.

candidates.name: Sync.me
candidates.why: Caller-ID exposure. Parsed name, email, and phone fields on the unsubscribe page, with a CAPTCHA marker. A processing-time sentence was not cleanly extracted. Direct GET worked.

candidates.name: Apollo Interactive
candidates.why: Simple parsed name, email, and message form for a marketing-site DSAR, with a CAPTCHA marker. Lower people-search exposure than the listing sites above. Included as a clean DSAR shape, not as a priority removal target.

candidates.name: UK open electoral register
candidates.why: Official GOV.UK guidance. Opt out through the register-to-vote service or the local electoral registration office. England, Scotland, Wales, Northern Ireland, and overseas voters are different contacts. The full register cannot be opted out. There is no single broker form to automate.

candidates.name: Canada National Do Not Call List
candidates.why: Official CRTC telemarketing registry, not a people-search deletion. Registration is free and telemarketers have 31 days. The consumer registration form fields were not parsed; phone and email contacts were. Useful for Canadian coverage and easy to confuse with broker removal.

candidates.name: DMAchoice
candidates.why: ANA mail-preference service. The fetched page is a login and registration form, not the preference form itself. Request types and the post-login steps are unknown. Include only as a marketing-mail choice, behind account creation.

candidates.name: Elections Canada
candidates.why: Official National Register of Electors opt-out. The page says to write to Elections Canada with name, date of birth, home and mailing addresses, and a signature. Opting out does not remove the right to vote, and the person must be added to the list again in order to vote. No web form was on the inspected page.

candidates.name: Elections Quebec
candidates.why: Élections Québec states three ways to be struck from the permanent list of electors: a mailed letter, the secure contact link, or a phone request for an application. Two supporting documents are required. The contact form was not opened. This is a voters-list process, not a broker deletion.

candidates.name: Elections BC
candidates.why: Elections BC says a person who believes distributed voter lists put their privacy or security at risk can call 1-800-661-8683 or write to the Director, Voter Data and Geography. The request omits name and address from those lists. It does not say the voter record is deleted.

candidates.name: Canada Post
candidates.why: Official advertising-mail page. Addressed mail that uses Canada Post lists can be stopped by phone at 1-800-267-1177 or by a linked database form that was not opened. Unaddressed mail is a note on the mailbox. Removal applies only to the current address, may take 10 business days, and addressed mail can continue for 90 days. Election mail and public-interest mail continue.

candidates.name: CMA Do Not Mail
candidates.why: The Canadian Marketing Association Do Not Mail page describes a free service that reduces personally addressed marketing mail. Register Now was not opened, so the fields are unknown. The 1-866 number on the page is the National Do Not Call List, not this mail registration. Same class of gap as DMAchoice: the service is real and the form is still uninspected.
